chapters.title: Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case
paragraphs: I was born in the year 18— to a large fortune, and gifted besides with fine natural abilities, inclined by temperament to hard work, and eager for the respect of the wise and good among my fellow men—so that, as you might expect, everything pointed to an honorable and distinguished future. And indeed the worst of my faults was a certain impatient high spirits, the kind that has made many a man happy, but which I found hard to reconcile with my burning wish to hold my head high and wear a more than usually grave face in public. So I fell into the habit of hiding my pleasures; and by the time I reached an age to reflect, and began to look around me and take stock of how far I had come and where I stood in the world, I found I was already committed to a profound double life. Many a man would even have boasted of the irregularities I was guilty of; but given the high standard I had set myself, I regarded them, and concealed them, with an almost morbid sense of shame. It was, then, less any particular depravity in my faults than the demanding nature of my ambitions that made me what I was, and cut a deeper trench in me than in most men between those provinces of good and evil that divide and compose a man’s dual nature. Because of this, I was driven to reflect long and constantly on that harsh law of life which lies at the root of religion and is one of the most abundant sources of human distress. Profound a double-dealer as I was, I was never in any sense a hypocrite; both sides of me were entirely in earnest. I was no less myself when I threw off restraint and plunged into shame than when I labored, in broad daylight, at advancing knowledge or relieving sorrow and suffering. And it happened that the direction of my scientific studies, which led wholly toward the mystical and the transcendental, reacted upon this and threw a strong light on my awareness of the endless war being waged among my own faculties. Day by day, from both sides of my mind—the moral and the intellectual—I drew steadily nearer to that truth whose partial discovery has doomed me to so dreadful a shipwreck: that man is not truly one, but truly two. I say two, only because the present state of my own knowledge does not go beyond that point. Others will come after me and take these same lines of inquiry further than I have; and I will hazard the guess that man will in the end be recognized as a mere confederation of many different, incongruous, and independent inhabitants. For my own part, given the nature of my life, I advanced unerringly in one direction, and one only. It was on the moral side, and in my own person, that I came to recognize the deep and original duality of man. I saw that of the two natures contending in the field of my consciousness, even if I could fairly be said to be either one, it was only because I was fundamentally both; and from an early date—even before my scientific discoveries had begun to suggest the bare possibility of such a miracle—I had taken to dwelling with pleasure, as on a cherished daydream, on the idea of separating these two elements. If each, I told myself, could be housed in a separate identity, life would be relieved of everything that made it unbearable: the unjust twin could go his own way, freed from the aspirations and the remorse of his more upright brother, while the just one could walk his upward path steadily and safely, doing the good deeds that gave him pleasure, and no longer exposed to disgrace and penitence at the hands of this alien evil within him. It was mankind’s curse that these two incongruous bundles should be bound together this way—that in the tormented womb of consciousness these opposing twins should be forever struggling. How, then, were they to be split apart?

I had gotten this far in my reflections when, as I said, a side light began to shine on the subject from my laboratory table. I began to perceive, more deeply than anyone had yet stated, the trembling immateriality, the mist-like transience, of this seemingly solid body we go about clothed in. I found certain agents to have the power to shake and pull back that fleshly garment, the way a wind might toss the curtains of a tent. For two good reasons, I will not go deeply into this scientific branch of my confession. First, because I have learned that the burden and doom of our life is bound forever to man’s shoulders, and that when we try to cast it off, it only comes back upon us with a stranger and more terrible weight. Second, because, as my account will make all too plain, my discoveries were incomplete. Let it be enough, then, to say that I came to recognize my natural body as no more than the aura and radiance given off by certain of the powers that made up my spirit—and that I managed to compound a drug by which these powers could be dethroned from their supremacy, and a second form and face substituted, one no less natural to me for being the expression, and bearing the stamp, of the lower elements in my soul.

I hesitated a long time before putting this theory to the test of practice. I knew well that I risked death; a drug with such power over the very fortress of identity might, through the least excess in dose or the least mistiming in taking it, utterly wipe out the immaterial dwelling it was meant only to alter. But in the end the temptation of so singular and profound a discovery overcame my fears. I had long since prepared my tincture; I bought at once, from a firm of wholesale chemists, a large quantity of a particular salt which my experiments told me was the last ingredient needed; and late one accursed night I mixed the elements together, watched them boil and smoke in the glass, and when the seething had died down, drank off the potion with a strong rush of courage.

The most wrenching pangs followed: a grinding in my bones, a deadly nausea, and a horror of the spirit that could not be surpassed at the hour of birth or death. Then these agonies began swiftly to subside, and I came back to myself as if out of a bad illness. There was something strange in my sensations, something indescribably new and, for its very novelty, unbelievably sweet. I felt younger, lighter, happier in body; inwardly I was aware of a heady recklessness, a current of disordered, sensual images racing through my mind like a millrace, a loosening of every bond of duty, an unfamiliar but not an innocent freedom of the soul. From the very first breath of this new life I knew myself to be more wicked—ten times more wicked—sold as a slave to my original evil; and the thought, in that moment, braced and delighted me like wine. I stretched out my hands, exulting in the freshness of these sensations; and in that very act, I suddenly realized that I had shrunk in height.

There was no mirror in my room at that date; the one that stands beside me now as I write was brought in later, for the very purpose of these transformations. The night, however, had worn on far into the morning—a morning that, black as it still was, was nearly ready to give birth to the day—and the household was locked in the deepest hours of sleep. Flushed as I was with hope and triumph, I decided to venture, in my new shape, as far as my own bedroom. I crossed the yard, where the stars looked down on me—I could almost have believed, with wonder, that I was the first creature of my kind their sleepless watch had ever disclosed to them. I stole through the corridors, a stranger in my own house; and reaching my room, I saw for the first time the face and form of Edward Hyde.

Here I can only speak from theory, telling you not what I know but what I suppose to be most likely. The evil side of my nature, to which I had now transferred the power of shaping the body, was less strong and less developed than the good side I had just deposed. Besides, in the course of my life—which had been, after all, nine-tenths a life of effort, virtue, and self-control—that evil side had been far less exercised and far less worn down. And that, I think, is why Edward Hyde was so much smaller, slighter, and younger than Henry Jekyll. Just as good shone plainly on the face of the one, evil was written broadly and openly on the face of the other. Evil, moreover—which I still believe to be the deadly side of man—had left on that body a stamp of deformity and decay. And yet when I looked at that ugly idol in the glass, I felt no revulsion, but rather a leap of welcome. This too was myself. It felt natural and human. To my eyes it carried a livelier image of the spirit; it seemed more direct and single than the imperfect, divided face I had until then been used to calling mine. And in that much I was doubtless right. I have noticed that when I wore the appearance of Edward Hyde, no one could come near me at first without a visible shrinking of the flesh. This, I take it, is because every human being we meet is a mixture of good and evil—while Edward Hyde, alone among the ranks of mankind, was pure evil.

I lingered only a moment at the mirror—the second and decisive experiment still had to be made. It remained to be seen whether I had lost my identity beyond recovery and would have to flee before daylight from a house that was no longer mine. Hurrying back to my cabinet, I once more prepared and drank the draught, once more suffered the pangs of dissolution, and came back to myself once more with the character, the stature, and the face of Henry Jekyll.

That night I had reached the fatal crossroads. Had I approached my discovery in a nobler spirit, had I risked the experiment while moved by generous or devout aspirations, everything would have turned out differently, and from these agonies of death and birth I would have emerged an angel instead of a fiend. The drug made no distinctions; it was neither devilish nor divine; it merely shook the doors of the prison that housed my nature, and what stood inside ran free—like the captives at Philippi, freed when the earthquake shook open their prison doors. At that time my virtue was asleep; my evil, kept wide awake by ambition, was alert and quick to seize its chance; and the thing that came forth was Edward Hyde. So although I now had two characters as well as two appearances, one was wholly evil, while the other was still the old Henry Jekyll—that incongruous mixture whose reform and improvement I had already given up hoping for. The movement, then, was entirely toward the worse.

Even then, I had not conquered my dislike of the dryness of a scholar’s life. I was still inclined to be merry at times, and since my pleasures were, to put it mildly, undignified—and I was not only well known and highly regarded but growing toward middle age—this contradiction in my life was daily becoming more unwelcome. It was on this front that my new power tempted me, until I fell into slavery to it. I had only to drink the draught, shed at once the body of the respected professor, and put on, like a heavy cloak, the body of Edward Hyde. I smiled at the idea; it struck me at the time as amusing, and I made my preparations with the most careful attention. I took and furnished that house in Soho where Hyde was later tracked down by the police, and hired as housekeeper a creature I knew well to be silent and unscrupulous. On the other side, I told my own servants that a Mr. Hyde, whom I described to them, was to have full liberty and authority about my house in the square; and to head off any mishap, I even called there in my second character, so as to make myself a familiar face. I then drew up that will you objected to so strongly, so that if anything befell me in the person of Dr. Jekyll, I could step into that of Edward Hyde without financial loss. And fortified, as I supposed, on every side, I began to take advantage of the strange immunity my position gave me.

Men have hired hitmen before now to carry out their crimes while their own person and reputation stayed safely sheltered. I was the first to do so for his pleasures. I was the first who could trudge along in the public eye weighed down by cheerful respectability, and then, in an instant, like a schoolboy, strip off these borrowed trappings and plunge headlong into a sea of freedom. But for me, wrapped in my impenetrable cloak, the safety was complete. Think of it—I did not even exist! Let me only slip through my laboratory door, give me only a second or two to mix and swallow the draught that I always kept standing ready, and whatever he had done, Edward Hyde would vanish like the mark of breath fading off a mirror; and there in his place, quietly at home, trimming the midnight lamp in his study, would be a man who could afford to laugh at suspicion—Henry Jekyll.

The pleasures I hurried to seek out in my disguise were, as I have said, undignified—I would hardly use a harsher word. But in the hands of Edward Hyde, they soon began to turn monstrous. When I came back from these excursions, I was often plunged into a kind of wonder at my own depravity, committed at second hand. This familiar spirit I had summoned out of my own soul, and sent out alone to do as it pleased, was a being inherently malicious and villainous; every act and thought of his was centered on himself; he drank pleasure with animal greed from any degree of pain inflicted on another, and was as relentless as a man made of stone. Henry Jekyll was at times appalled at the acts of Edward Hyde; but the situation stood outside the ordinary laws, and it insidiously loosened the grip of conscience. It was Hyde, after all, and Hyde alone, who was guilty. Jekyll was none the worse for it; he woke again to his good qualities seemingly unimpaired, and would even hurry, wherever possible, to undo the harm Hyde had done. And so his conscience slept on.

I have no intention of going into the details of the wickedness I thus connived at—for even now I can hardly bring myself to admit that I committed it. I mean only to point out the warnings and the successive stages by which my punishment drew nearer. I met with one incident which, since it led to no lasting consequence, I will do no more than mention. An act of cruelty to a child roused against me the anger of a passer-by, whom I recognized the other day in the person of your own kinsman; the doctor and the child’s family took his side; there were moments when I feared for my life; and at last, to pacify their entirely justified resentment, Edward Hyde had to bring them to the door and pay them with a cheque drawn in the name of Henry Jekyll. But this danger was easily removed for the future by opening an account at another bank in the name of Edward Hyde himself; and once I had given my double a signature by slanting my own handwriting backward, I believed myself safely beyond the reach of fate.

About two months before the murder of Sir Danvers, I had been out on one of my adventures, had come home at a late hour, and woke the next day in bed with somewhat strange sensations. It was no use my looking around me; no use seeing the decent furniture and the tall proportions of my room in the square; no use recognizing the pattern of the bed-curtains and the design of the mahogany frame—something kept insisting that I was not where I was, that I had not woken where I seemed to be, but in the little room in Soho where I was used to sleeping in the body of Edward Hyde. I smiled to myself, and, in my curious analytical way, began lazily inquiring into the makings of this illusion, occasionally drifting back, even as I did so, into a comfortable morning doze. I was still occupied this way when, in one of my more wakeful moments, my eye fell on my hand. Now the hand of Henry Jekyll—as you have often remarked—was professional in shape and size: large, firm, white, and well formed. But the hand I now saw clearly enough, in the yellow light of a mid-London morning, lying half-closed on the bedclothes, was lean, corded, knuckly, of a dusky pallor, and thickly shaded with dark hair. It was the hand of Edward Hyde.

I must have stared at it for nearly half a minute, sunk in the sheer stupidity of astonishment, before terror woke in my chest as suddenly and startlingly as the crash of cymbals; and bounding out of bed, I rushed to the mirror. At the sight that met my eyes, my blood turned into something exquisitely thin and icy. Yes—I had gone to bed Henry Jekyll; I had woken up Edward Hyde. How was this to be explained? I asked myself; and then, with another leap of terror—how was it to be undone? It was well on in the morning; the servants were up; all my drugs were in the cabinet—a long journey down two flights of stairs, through the back passage, across the open courtyard, and through the dissecting theatre, from where I now stood, struck with horror. It might indeed be possible to cover my face, but what use was that when I could not conceal the change in my stature? And then, with an overpowering sweetness of relief, it came back to me that the servants were already used to the comings and goings of my second self. I soon dressed, as best I could, in clothes of my own size; soon passed through the house, where Bradshaw stared and drew back at the sight of Mr. Hyde at such an hour and in such strange attire; and ten minutes later, Dr. Jekyll had returned to his own shape and was sitting down, with a darkened brow, to make a show of eating breakfast.

My appetite was small indeed. This inexplicable incident, this reversal of everything I had previously experienced, seemed, like the finger that wrote on the wall in Babylon, to be spelling out the letters of my judgment; and I began to reflect more seriously than ever on the questions and possibilities raised by my double existence. That part of me which I had the power of projecting outward had lately been much exercised and nourished; it had seemed to me of late as though the body of Edward Hyde had grown in stature, as though, when I wore that form, I were conscious of a richer flow of blood; and I began to make out a danger that, if this went on much longer, the balance of my nature might be permanently overturned, the power of changing at will forfeited, and the character of Edward Hyde become irrevocably mine. The power of the drug had not always shown itself equally. Once, very early in my career, it had failed me altogether; since then I had been obliged on more than one occasion to double the dose, and once, at infinite risk of death, to treble it; and these rare uncertainties had until now cast the only shadow over my contentment. Now, however, in the light of that morning’s accident, I was led to notice that whereas, in the beginning, the difficulty had been to throw off the body of Jekyll, it had of late gradually but decidedly shifted to the other side. Everything, then, seemed to point to this: that I was slowly losing my grip on my original and better self, and slowly merging into my second and worse one.

Between these two I now felt I had to choose. My two natures shared memory in common, but every other faculty was most unequally divided between them. Jekyll—who was the composite of the two—now with the most sensitive misgivings, now with a greedy relish, projected himself into and shared in the pleasures and adventures of Hyde; but Hyde was indifferent to Jekyll, or remembered him only as a mountain bandit remembers the cave where he hides from pursuit. Jekyll had more than a father’s interest in Hyde; Hyde had more than a son’s indifference to Jekyll. To cast my lot with Jekyll was to die to those appetites I had long secretly indulged and had of late begun to pamper. To cast it with Hyde was to die to a thousand interests and ambitions, and to become, in a single stroke and forever, despised and friendless. The bargain might look uneven, but there was still another weight on the scale: while Jekyll would suffer sharply in the fires of self-denial, Hyde would not even be conscious of all he had lost. Strange as my circumstances were, the terms of this debate are as old and ordinary as mankind itself; much the same temptations and fears decide the matter for any trembling, tempted sinner; and it turned out with me, as it turns out with the vast majority of my fellow men, that I chose the better course and then lacked the strength to hold to it.

Yes, I preferred the aging and discontented doctor, surrounded by friends and cherishing honest hopes, and said a resolute farewell to the freedom, the relative youth, the light step, the leaping impulses, and the secret pleasures I had enjoyed in Hyde’s disguise. I made this choice, perhaps, with some unconscious reservation, for I neither gave up the house in Soho nor destroyed Edward Hyde’s clothes, which still lay ready in my cabinet. For two months, however, I stayed true to my resolve; for two months I led a life of such strictness as I had never managed before, and enjoyed the rewards of an approving conscience. But time at last began to wear away the freshness of my alarm; the praise of my own conscience began to feel routine; I began to be tormented with pangs and longings, as of Hyde straining after freedom; and at last, in a moment of moral weakness, I once again compounded and swallowed the transforming draught.

I don’t suppose that when a drunkard reasons with himself about his vice, he is troubled by the dangers he runs, through his brutish physical numbness, even one time out of five hundred; and no more had I, much as I had thought over my position, made enough allowance for the complete moral numbness and mindless readiness for evil that were the leading traits of Edward Hyde. Yet it was by these that I was punished. My devil had been caged a long time; he came out roaring. Even as I took the draught, I was aware of a more unrestrained, more furious tendency toward wickedness. It must have been this, I suppose, that stirred in my soul that storm of impatience with which I listened to the polite words of my unfortunate victim. I declare, at least, before God, that no morally sane man could have been guilty of that crime on so trivial a provocation, and that I struck no more reasonably than a sick child might break a toy. But I had voluntarily stripped myself of all those balancing instincts by which even the worst of us manages to walk with some degree of steadiness among temptations; and in my case, to be tempted at all, however slightly, was to fall.

Instantly the spirit of hell woke in me and raged. In a transport of glee I beat the unresisting body, tasting delight in every blow; and it was not until weariness had begun to set in that I was suddenly, at the very height of my delirium, struck through the heart by a cold thrill of terror. A mist cleared; I saw that my life was forfeit, and fled from the scene of these excesses, glorying and trembling at once, my appetite for evil satisfied and stirred up further, my love of life wound up to its highest pitch. I ran to the house in Soho and, to make doubly sure, destroyed my papers; from there I set out through the lamplit streets, in that same divided ecstasy of mind, gloating over my crime, light-headedly plotting others for the future, and yet all the while hurrying on and listening behind me for the footsteps of my pursuer. Hyde had a song on his lips as he mixed the draught, and as he drank it, toasted the dead man. The pangs of transformation had not finished tearing at him before Henry Jekyll, streaming with tears of gratitude and remorse, had fallen to his knees and lifted his clasped hands to God. The veil of self-indulgence was torn from top to bottom. I saw my whole life laid out before me: I followed it back to the days of childhood, when I had walked holding my father’s hand, and forward through the self-denying labors of my professional life, arriving again and again, with the same sense of unreality, at the accursed horrors of that evening. I could have screamed aloud; I tried with tears and prayers to smother the crowd of hideous images and sounds that swarmed against my memory; and still, between one prayer and the next, the ugly face of my wickedness stared into my soul. As the sharpness of this remorse began to fade, it was followed by a sense of joy. The problem of my conduct was solved. Hyde was impossible from now on; whether I wished it or not, I was now confined to the better part of my existence—and oh, how I rejoiced to think of it! With what willing humility I embraced once more the restrictions of ordinary life! With what heartfelt renunciation I locked the door through which I had so often come and gone, and ground the key under my heel!

The next day came the news that the murder had not gone unnoticed, that Hyde’s guilt was plain to the whole world, and that the victim had been a man highly regarded in public life. It had not only been a crime—it had been a tragic act of folly. I believe I was glad to know it; I believe I was glad to have my better impulses thus reinforced and guarded by the terrors of the gallows. Jekyll was now my city of refuge; let Hyde so much as peep out for an instant, and the hands of every man would be raised to seize and kill him.

I resolved that my future conduct would make up for the past, and I can honestly say that this resolve bore some good fruit. You know yourself how earnestly, in the last months of last year, I labored to relieve suffering; you know that much was done for others, and that the days passed quietly, almost happily, for myself. Nor can I truthfully say that I grew tired of this beneficial, innocent life; I think, rather, that I enjoyed it more fully with each day; but I was still cursed with my divided purpose, and as the first sharpness of my penitence wore off, the lower side of me—so long indulged, so recently chained down—began to growl for its freedom. Not that I dreamed of bringing Hyde back to life; the mere idea of that would startle me into a frenzy. No—it was in my own person that I was once more tempted to trifle with my conscience, and it was as an ordinary secret sinner that I finally gave way before the assaults of temptation.

There is an end to all things; the largest vessel fills up at last; and this brief surrender to my evil side finally destroyed the balance of my soul. And yet I was not alarmed; the fall felt natural, like a return to the old days before I had made my discovery. It was a fine, clear January day, wet underfoot where the frost had melted, but cloudless overhead; and Regent’s Park was full of winter birdsong and sweet with the smell of spring. I sat in the sun on a bench; the animal in me licking the memory of its meal; the spiritual side a little drowsy, promising penitence to come but not yet moved to begin it. After all, I reflected, I was just like my neighbors; and then I smiled, comparing myself to other men, comparing my active good will with the lazy cruelty of their neglect. And at the very moment of that vain, self-congratulating thought, a wave of sickness came over me—a horrible nausea and the most deadly shuddering. These passed, and left me faint; and then, as the faintness in turn subsided, I began to be aware of a change in the temper of my thoughts: a greater boldness, a contempt for danger, a loosening of every bond of duty. I looked down; my clothes hung shapeless on my shrunken limbs; the hand resting on my knee was corded and hairy. I was once more Edward Hyde. A moment before I had been secure in every man’s respect, wealthy, well-loved—with the table being laid for me in my own dining room at home—and now I was the common prey of mankind, hunted, homeless, a known murderer, forfeit to the gallows.

My reason wavered, but it did not fail me completely. I have more than once noticed that in my second character my faculties seemed honed to a fine point, and my spirits more tightly wound; and so it came about that where Jekyll might perhaps have given way, Hyde rose to meet the moment. My drugs were in one of the cupboards of my cabinet—how was I to reach them? That was the problem I set myself to solve, crushing my temples in my hands. I had shut the laboratory door. If I tried to get in through the house, my own servants would deliver me to the gallows. I saw I would have to use another man’s hands, and thought of Lanyon. How was he to be reached? How persuaded? Supposing I escaped capture in the streets, how was I to get into his presence? And how was I—an unknown, unpleasant-looking visitor—to persuade the famous physician to go rifling through the study of his colleague, Dr. Jekyll? Then I remembered that one part of my original character remained to me: I could still write in my own hand; and once that spark had caught, the path I had to follow lit up from end to end.

So I arranged my clothes as best I could, hailed a passing hansom cab, and drove to a hotel on Portland Street, whose name I happened to remember. At the sight of me—comical enough, however tragic a fate these clothes covered—the driver could not hide his amusement. I gnashed my teeth at him in a gust of devilish fury, and the smile withered from his face—luckily for him, but even more luckily for myself, for in another instant I would certainly have dragged him down from his seat. Entering the hotel, I looked about me with so black a face that the staff trembled; they did not exchange a single glance in my presence, but took my orders obsequiously, led me to a private room, and brought me the means to write. Hyde in danger of his life was a creature new to me: shaken with excessive rage, wound up to the pitch of murder, hungry to inflict pain. Yet the creature was cunning; he mastered his fury with a great effort of will, composed his two important letters—one to Lanyon and one to Poole—and, so as to have real proof that they had been sent, had them mailed by registered post. From then on he sat all day over the fire in the private room, gnawing his nails; he dined there, sitting alone with his fears, the waiter visibly quailing under his eye; and from there, once night had fully fallen, he set out in the corner of a closed cab and was driven back and forth through the streets of the city. He, I say—I cannot say I. That child of Hell had nothing human in him; nothing lived in him but fear and hatred. And when at last, believing the driver had begun to grow suspicious, he dismissed the cab and ventured out on foot, dressed in his ill-fitting clothes, a marked object among the crowds of the night, these two base passions raged inside him like a storm. He walked fast, hunted by his own fears, muttering to himself, slinking through the less-frequented streets, counting the minutes that still stood between him and midnight. Once a woman spoke to him—offering, I think, a box of matches. He struck her in the face, and she fled.

When I came back to myself at Lanyon’s, my old friend’s horror perhaps affected me somewhat—I don’t know; it was at any rate no more than a drop in the ocean beside the loathing with which I now look back on those hours. A change had come over me. It was no longer the fear of the gallows but the horror of being Hyde that tormented me. I received Lanyon’s condemnation half in a dream; it was half in a dream that I made my way home and got into bed. After the day’s exhaustion, I slept a tight, deep sleep that not even the nightmares that wracked me could break. I woke in the morning shaken and weakened, but refreshed. I still hated and feared the thought of the brute sleeping within me, and I had, of course, not forgotten the appalling dangers of the day before; but I was once more at home, in my own house and close to my drugs, and gratitude for my escape shone so brightly in my soul that it almost rivaled the brightness of hope.

I was crossing the courtyard at a leisurely pace after breakfast, enjoying the chill of the air, when I was seized again by those indescribable sensations that warned of the change coming on; and I had only just enough time to reach the shelter of my cabinet before I was once again raging and freezing with the passions of Hyde. On this occasion it took a double dose to bring me back to myself; and, alas, six hours later, as I sat looking sadly into the fire, the pangs returned, and the drug had to be given again. In short, from that day forward it seemed to take a great effort—something like an athlete’s—and only the immediate spur of the drug, for me to be able to wear the face of Jekyll at all. At every hour of day and night I might be seized by the warning shudder; above all, if I slept, or even dozed off for a moment in my chair, it was always as Hyde that I woke. Under the strain of this constantly looming doom, and from the sleeplessness to which I now condemned myself—sleeplessness beyond what I would have thought possible for a man to endure—I became, in my own person, a creature consumed and hollowed out by fever, weak and listless in both body and mind, occupied by a single thought: the horror of my other self. But when I slept, or when the medicine’s power wore off, I would leap almost without any transition—for the pangs of transformation grew less marked with each day—into a state of mind brimming with images of terror, a soul boiling with causeless hatreds, and a body that seemed too weak to contain the raging energies of life within it. The powers of Hyde seemed to have grown as the health of Jekyll declined. And certainly the hatred that now divided them was equal on both sides. For Jekyll, it was a matter of pure survival instinct. He had now seen the full deformity of that creature who shared with him some part of consciousness, and who was his co-heir to death; and beyond these bonds of shared existence—which were in themselves the most painful part of his distress—he thought of Hyde, for all his vigor and energy, as something not merely hellish but inanimate. This was the shocking thing: that the slime of the pit seemed to cry out and speak; that shapeless dust gestured and sinned; that what was dead, and had no form, should usurp the functions of the living. And this too: that this rebellious horror was bound to him closer than a wife, closer than his own eye; that it lay caged in his flesh, where he heard it mutter and felt it struggle to be born; and that at every hour of weakness, and whenever sleep left him unguarded, it overpowered him and thrust him out of his own life. Hyde’s hatred of Jekyll was of a different kind. His terror of the gallows drove him continually to commit a kind of temporary suicide, returning himself to his subordinate standing as a part rather than a whole person; but he hated the necessity of it, he hated the despair into which Jekyll had now fallen, and he resented the dislike with which he himself was regarded. Hence the ape-like tricks he would play on me—scrawling blasphemies in my own handwriting across the pages of my books, burning my letters, and destroying the portrait of my father; and indeed, had it not been for his fear of death, he would long ago have ruined himself in order to drag me down with him. But his love of life is remarkable. I will go further: I, who sicken and turn cold at the mere thought of him—when I recall the abject, passionate force of this attachment to life, and when I know how he fears my power to cut him off by suicide—I find it in my heart to pity him.

It is pointless, and time terribly fails me, to prolong this description; let it be enough to say that no one has ever suffered such torments. And yet even to these, habit brought—not relief, no—but a certain callousness of soul, a certain acquiescence in despair; and my punishment might have gone on for years, but for the final calamity that has now fallen, and that has at last severed me from my own face and nature for good. My supply of the salt, which had never been renewed since the date of the first experiment, began to run low. I sent out for a fresh supply and mixed the draught; the seething followed, and the first change of color, but not the second; I drank it, and it had no effect. You will learn from Poole how I have had all London searched; it was useless; and I am now convinced that my original supply was impure, and that it was that unknown impurity which gave the draught its power.

About a week has passed, and I am now finishing this statement under the influence of the last of the old powders. This, then—short of a miracle—is the last time that Henry Jekyll will be able to think his own thoughts, or see his own face, now so sadly changed, in the glass. Nor must I delay too long in bringing my writing to a close, for if this account has escaped destruction so far, it has been through a combination of great caution and great good luck. Should the throes of the change seize me in the act of writing it, Hyde will tear it to pieces; but if some time passes after I have set it aside, his remarkable selfishness and his confinement to the present moment will probably save it once again from his ape-like spite. And indeed the doom now closing in on both of us has already changed and crushed him. Half an hour from now, when I shall put on that hated personality again, and forever, I know that I will sit shuddering and weeping in my chair, or else continue, in the most strained and fear-stricken ecstasy of listening, to pace up and down this room—my last refuge on earth—straining to hear every sound of menace. Will Hyde die on the scaffold? Or will he find the courage to release himself at the last moment? God knows; I no longer care. This is my true hour of death, and what follows concerns someone other than myself. Here, then, as I lay down the pen and set about sealing up my confession, I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end.
